deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous page of German lecture or reading notes on the history of Ptolemaic Egypt, continuing from the previous page (Philadelphus, Evergetes) and leading into the next (Epiphanes' later reign, Philometor and Physkon). The hand, a neat schoolroom Kurrent, does not look like Gauss's own; it is plausibly a family member's or a student's notebook bound into the Nachlass.

The content, by sentence:

(1) Ptolemy IV Philopator reigned 221–204 BC. He courted the friendship of the Romans. He had a dangerous neighbour in Antiochus III the Great, was drawn into war with him and defeated him at 'Ravia', i.e. Raphia (217 BC, Fourth Syrian War).

(2) He was under the 'Vormundschaft' (tutelage) of Sosibius. His wife was his sister (Arsinoe III). He died in 204 (written '+204').

(3) His son and successor was Ptolemy V Epiphanes, who also came under the guardianship of Sosibius. Sosibius shared the business of government with Tlepolemus, but the two could not get along.

(4) In 203 Antiochus attacked for the second time. The Egyptians turned to Rome and conferred the guardianship on the Senate. The Senate sent Marcus [Aemilius] Lepidus (written 'Lebitus'), who entrusted the administration to Aristomenes.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Historical: Philopator was an adult (about 23) at his accession in 221. Sosibius was his chief minister, not his guardian. 'Vormundschaft' is the note-taker's or lecturer's simplification.

Historical: under Epiphanes the regency was first held by Agathocles together with Sosibius. Tlepolemus rose after Agathocles' fall (c. 203/202), and Sosibius died around then. The pairing 'Sosibius and Tlepolemus' compresses events; an alternative reading is Sosibius the Younger, who did share power with Tlepolemus.
Historical: Antiochus III's invasion that began the Fifth Syrian War is usually dated 202/201 BC, not 203.

Historical: the story that the Senate was made guardian (tutor) of Ptolemy V and sent M. Aemilius Lepidus comes from Justin and Valerius Maximus. Modern historians regard it as largely legendary or exaggerated. Lepidus was one of the Roman envoys of 201/200 BC.
Orthography: 'Ravia' for Raphia, 'Lebitus' for Lepidus, and 'griff ... zum 2ten mal' is missing the particle 'an'. These are slips of the note-taker.

results.what: Historical notes on Ptolemy IV Philopator and the early reign of Ptolemy V Epiphanes (Raphia, Sosibius, Tlepolemus, Roman embassy of Lepidus, Aristomenes)
results.modern_name: Hellenistic/Ptolemaic history (Fourth and Fifth Syrian Wars)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard ancient sources (Polybius, Justin) as relayed in early-19th-century history textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical schoolbook or lecture material on Ptolemaic Egypt, with no mathematical content. The handwriting does not appear to be Gauss's own, so it is likely notes by a family member or student kept among his papers. Nothing here bears on Gauss's mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Philopator's reign as given (221–204 BC) lasts 17 years.
Consistent with the previous page: Evergetes reigned from 246 to 221 BC, i.e. 25 years ('Regierte 25 Jahr').

transcription_corrections: 'Ravia[?]' is clearly written 'Ravia' and means Raphia (battle of 217 BC).
'Tlepolemus[?]' is confirmed as Tlepolemus (written with a struck or overwritten initial, 'T(l)epolemus').
'Marcus Lebitus[?]' is written 'Marcus Lebitus' and stands for Marcus (Aemilius) Lepidus.
'Die Aegypter' is written 'Aegyptier' in the manuscript.
'203 griff Antiochus zum 2ten mal' is as written; the separable particle 'an' is omitted in the manuscript.
